questions.question: Two wires of same length and radius are joined end to end and loaded. The Young's moduli of the materials of the two wires are ${Y}_{1}$ and ${Y}_{2}$. The combination behaves as a single wire then its Young's modulus is:
questions.explanation:
In series combination, $\Delta l = {ℓ}_{1} + {ℓ}_{2} Y = \frac{F / A}{\Delta ℓ / ℓ} \implies \Delta ℓ = \frac{Fℓ}{AY} \implies \Delta ℓ \propto \frac{ℓ}{Y}$

Equivalent length of rod after joining is $= 2ℓ$

As, lengths are same and force is also same in series

$\Delta ℓ = \Delta {ℓ}_{1} + \Delta {ℓ}_{2} \frac{{ℓ}_{\mathrm{eq}}}{{Y}_{\mathrm{eq}}} = \frac{ℓ}{{Y}_{1}} + \frac{ℓ}{{Y}_{2}} \implies \frac{2ℓ}{Y} = \frac{ℓ}{{Y}_{1}} + \frac{ℓ}{{Y}_{2}} ∴Y = \frac{2{Y}_{1}{Y}_{2}}{{Y}_{1} + {Y}_{2}}$

questions.question: Young’s moduli of the material of wires A and B are in the ratio of $1 : 4$, while its area of cross sections are in the ratio of $1 : 3$. If the same amount of load is applied to both the wires, the amount of elongation produced in the wires A and B will be in the ratio of [Assume length of wires A and B are same]
questions.explanation:
The formula to calculate the elongation of a metallic wire because of the application of a load can be written as

$\begin{matrix}\Delta L = \left(\frac{FL}{AY}\right)\end{matrix}...\left(1\right)$

The ratio of the elongations for both the wires is, then, calculated as follows-

$\begin{matrix}\frac{ \Delta {L}_{1}}{ \Delta {L}_{2}} & = & \frac{\frac{FL}{{A}_{1}{Y}_{1}}}{\frac{FL}{{A}_{2}}} \\ & = & \frac{{A}_{2}{Y}_{2}}{{A}_{1}{Y}_{1}} \\ & = & \frac{3}{1} \times \frac{4}{1} \\ & = & \frac{12}{1}\end{matrix}$

questions.question: The elastic limit of brass is $379MPa$. The minimum diameter of a brass rod if it is to support a $400N$ load without exceeding its elastic limit will be

Stress $= \frac{F}{A}$

Elastic limit is $379\text{ }MPa \implies 379 \times {10}^{6} = \frac{400}{A} = \frac{400}{\pi {d}^{2} / 4} d = \sqrt{\frac{400 \times 4}{\pi \times 379 \times {10}^{6}}} = 1.16 \times {10}^{ - 3}\text{ }m = 1.16\text{ }mm$

questions.question: The length of metallic wire is ${l}_{1}$ when tension in it is ${T}_{1}$. It is ${l}_{2}$ when the tension is ${T}_{2}$. The original length of the wire will be :
questions.explanation:
Assuming Hooke's law to be valid

$T \propto \left(\Delta ℓ\right) T = k\left(\Delta ℓ\right)$

Let,${ℓ}_{0} =$ natural length (original length) $\implies T = k\left(ℓ - {ℓ}_{0}\right)$

so, ${T}_{1} = k\left({ℓ}_{1} - {ℓ}_{0}\right) & {T}_{2} = k\left({ℓ}_{2} - {ℓ}_{0}\right) \implies \frac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \frac{{ℓ}_{1} - {ℓ}_{0}}{{ℓ}_{2} - {ℓ}_{0}} \implies {ℓ}_{0} = \frac{{T}_{2}{ℓ}_{1} - {T}_{1}{ℓ}_{2}}{{T}_{2} - {T}_{1}}$

.

questions.question: Two wires A and B are made of same material having ratio of lengths $\frac{L_A}{L_B}=\frac{1}{3}$ and their diameters ratio $\frac{d_A}{d_B}=2$. If both the wires are stretched using same force, what would be the ratio of their respective elongations?
questions.explanation:
$\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2 \Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}$

Given, $F_A=F_B$ and $Y_A=Y_B \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}}{\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right) \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{B}}^2}{\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{A}}^2}\right)=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right)^2 \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{12}$

questions.question: If $Y,K$ and $\eta$ are the values of Young's modulus, bulk modulus and modulus of rigidity of any material respectively. Choose the correct relation for these parameters.
questions.explanation:
$Y -$Young's modulus, $K -$Bulk modulus, $\eta -$modulus of rigidity

We know that,

$Y = 3k\left(1 - 2\sigma \right) \implies \sigma = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{Y}{3k}\right)...\left(1\right) \implies Y = 2\eta \left(1 + \sigma \right) \implies \sigma = \frac{Y}{2\eta } - 1...\left(2\right)$

From the equation $\left(1\right)$ and the equation $\left(2\right) \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{Y}{3k}\right) = \frac{Y}{2\eta } - 1 \implies 1 - \frac{Y}{3k} = \frac{Y}{\eta } - 2 \implies \frac{Y}{3k} = 3 - \frac{Y}{n} \implies \frac{Y}{3k} = \frac{3\eta - Y}{\eta } \implies \frac{\eta Y}{3k} = 3\eta - Y \implies k = \frac{\eta Y}{9\eta - 3Y}N{m}^{ - 2}$.

questions.question: The Young's modulus of a steel wire of length $6m$ and cross-sectional area $3{\mathrm{mm}}^{2}$, is $2 \times {11}^{11}N / {m}^{2}$ . The wire is suspended from its support on a given planet. A block of mass $4\mathrm{kg}$ is attached to the free end of the wire. The acceleration due to gravity on the planet is $\frac{1}{4}$ of its value on the earth. The elongation of wire is (Take $g$ on the earth $= 10m / {s}^{2}$ ):
questions.explanation:
The external force or tension $\left(F\right)$ acting on the wire is its own weight. It is given by

$\begin{matrix}F & = & mg \\ = 4\mathrm{kg} \times \frac{10}{4}m{s}^{ - 2} \\ = 10N \\ \end{matrix}$

The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the wire is given by

$\begin{matrix}Y & = & \frac{\frac{F}{A}}{\frac{ \Delta L}{L}} \\ = \frac{FL}{ \Delta LA}..........................(1)\end{matrix}$

where, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $L$ is the original length and $\Delta L$ is the elongation of the wire.

Substitute the given values of the known parameters into equation (1) and solve to calculate the required elongation of the wire.

$\begin{matrix}2 \times {10}^{11}N / {m}^{2} & = & \frac{10N \times 6m}{ \Delta L \times 3{\mathrm{mm}}^{2} \times \frac{1{m}^{2}}{{10}^{6}{\mathrm{mm}}^{2}}} \\ \Delta L & = & \frac{10N \times 6m}{2 \times {10}^{11}N / {m}^{2} \times 3{\mathrm{mm}}^{2} \times \frac{1{m}^{2}}{{10}^{6}{\mathrm{mm}}^{2}}} \\ = 0.0001m \times \frac{{10}^{3}\mathrm{mm}}{1m} \\ = 0.1\mathrm{mm}\end{matrix}$

The stress required to produce a net elongation of $0.2mm$ is,

[Given, the Young's Modulus for steel and brass are, respectively, $120 \times {10}^{9}N / {m}^{2}$ and $60 \times {10}^{9}N / {m}^{2}$ ]

Stress will be same in both rods

And

$\Delta {l}_{1} + \Delta {l}_{2} = 0.2 \times {10}^{ - 3}m$ … (2)

From equation (1) and (2)

Stress $\times \left(\frac{l}{{Y}_{1}} + \frac{l}{{Y}_{2}}\right) = 0.2 \times {10}^{ - 3}m$

questions.question: Speed of a transverse wave on a straight wire (mass $6.0g,$ length $60cm$ and area of cross-section $1.0m{m}^{2}$ is $90{ms}^{ - 1}$. If the Young's modulus of wire is $16 \times {10}^{11}N{m}^{ - 2}$, the extension of wire over its natural length is:

After substituting value of $\mu ,v,l,A$ and $Y$ we get

$\Delta l = 0.3mm$

questions.question: An aluminium rod with Young’s modulus $Y = 7.0 \times {10}^{10}N{m}^{ - 2}$ undergoes elastic strain of $0.04%$. The energy per unit volume stored in the rod in $\mathrm{SI}$ unit

The energy per unit volume can be written from equation (i)

$\frac{E}{V} = \frac{Y}{2} \times {\left(\frac{ \Delta }{l}\right)}^{2}...(ii)$

Substituting the values in equation (ii)

$\frac{E}{V} = \frac{1}{2} \times 7 \times {10}^{10} \times \frac{0.04 \times 0.04}{{10}^{4}} = 56 \times {10}^{2}$

questions.question: Young's moduli of two wires $A$ and $B$ are in the ratio $7 : 4$ . Wire $A$ is $2m$ long and has radius $R.$ Wire $B$ is $1.5m$ long and has radius $2mm.$ If the two wires stretch by the same length for a given load, the value of $R$ is close to:

Stress $= F / A$

questions.question: Under the same load, wire A having length $5.0m$ and cross section $2.5 \times {10}^{ - 5}{m}^{2}$ stretches uniformly by the same amount as another wire $B$ of length $6.0m$ and a cross section of $3.0 \times {10}^{ - 5}{m}^{2}$ stretches. Elongation in uniform wire under load is given by, $\Delta l = \frac{Fl}{SY},$ where $S$ is area of cross-section.

As $F$ is same for both wire and $\Delta l$ is also same, we can write

$\frac{\Delta l}{F} = \frac{l}{SY}\; \implies \frac{5}{\left(2.5 \times {10}^{ - 5}\right) \times {Y}_{A}} = \frac{6}{\left(3 \times {10}^{ - 5}\right) \times {Y}_{B}} \implies \frac{{Y}_{A}}{{Y}_{B}} = 1$

questions.question: A wire of length $L$ and radius $r$ is clamped at one end. If its other end is pulled by a force $F$, its length increases by $l$. If the radius of the wire and the applied force both are reduced to half of their original values keeping original length constant, the increase in length will become:
questions.explanation:
The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the wire, in the first case, can be written as

$Y = \frac{\frac{F}{\pi {r}^{2}}}{\frac{l}{L}}...\left(1\right)$

From equation (1), it follows that

$F = Y\pi {r}^{2} \times \frac{l}{L}...\left(2\right)$

For the second case, the Young's modulus is given by

$Y = \frac{\frac{F / 2}{\pi {r}^{2} / 4}}{\frac{l'}{L}}...\left(3\right)$

From equation (3), it follows that

$F = Y\frac{l'}{L} \times 2 \times \frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{4}...\left(4\right)$

From equations (2) and (4), it implies that

$Y\pi {r}^{2} \times \frac{l}{L} = Y\frac{l'}{L} \times 2 \times \frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{4}\;$

;

questions.question:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R)

**Assertion (A)** : The property of body, by virtue of which it tends to regain its original shape when the external force is removed, is Elasticity.

**Reason (R)** : The restoring force depends upon the bonded inter atomic and inter molecular force of solid.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
Elasticity is the ability of a material to deform under stress and then return to its original shape when the stress is removed.

The restoring force in elastic materials is associated with the inter-atomic or inter-molecular forces that act to bring the atoms or molecules back to their original positions when the material is deformed. When an external force is applied to a material, it causes a displacement of atoms or molecules from their equilibrium positions. The restoring force is a result of the potential energy stored in these inter-atomic or inter-molecular bonds, and it works to bring the material back to its original state.

Hence, both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation (A)

questions.question: The area of cross-section of a railway track is $0.01{m}^{2}.$ The temperature variation is $10 ^\circ C.$ Coefficient of linear expansion of material of track is ${10}^{ - 5}C - 1∘.$ The energy stored per meter in the track is $J{m}^{ - 1}.$ (Young's modulus of material of track is ${10}^{11}N{m}^{ - 2}$)
questions.explanation:
Elastic energy $= \frac{Y}{2}(\mathrm{strain}{)}^{2} \times$ Area $\times$ length

$\implies$ Elastic energy per unit length $= \frac{Y}{2}(\mathrm{strain}{)}^{2} \times$ Area

$($strain $= \frac{\Delta ℓ}{ℓ} = \alpha \Delta T = {10}^{ - 5} \times 10 = {10}^{ - 4}) = \frac{{10}^{11}}{2} \times {\left({10}^{ - 4}\right)}^{2} \times {10}^{ - 2} = 5J{m}^{ - 1}$

questions.question: The elastic potential energy stored in a steel wire of length $20m$ stretched through $2\mathrm{cm}$ is $80J.$ The cross sectional area of the wire is _____ ${\mathrm{mm}}^{2}.$ (Given, $Y = 2.0 \times {10}^{11}N{m}^{–2}$)
questions.explanation:
The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material is given by

$\begin{matrix}Y & = & \frac{\mathrm{stress}}{\mathrm{strain}} \\ & = & \frac{\mathrm{stress}}{\frac{ \Delta l}{L}}...\left(1\right)\end{matrix}$

The formula to calculate the potential energy $\left(U\right)$ stored into the wire is given by

$\begin{matrix}U & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{stress} \times \mathrm{strain} \times \mathrm{volume} \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{stress} \times \frac{ \Delta l}{L} \times A \times L \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{stress} \times A \times \Delta l...\left(2\right)\end{matrix}$

From equation (1) and equation (2), it can be written that

$U = \frac{1}{2} \times Y \times \frac{{\left( \Delta l\right)}^{2}}{L} \times A...\left(3\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) and solve to calculate the required cross-sectional area of the wire.

$\begin{matrix}80J & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times {10}^{11}{\mathrm{Nm}}^{ - 2} \times \frac{{\left(0.02m\right)}^{2}}{20m} \times A \\ & \implies & A = \frac{2 \times 80J \times 20}{2.0 \times {10}^{11} \times 4 \times {10}^{ - 4}{\mathrm{Nm}}^{ - 1}} \\ & = & 4 \times {10}^{ - 5}{m}^{2} \times \frac{{10}^{6}{\mathrm{mm}}^{2}}{1{m}^{2}} \\ & = & 40{\mathrm{mm}}^{2}\end{matrix}$

questions.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and Young's modulus $2.0 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$ is stretched by a force. If Poisson ratio and transverse strain for the wire are 0.2 and $10^{-3}$ respectively, then the elastic potential energy density of the wire is _______ $\times 10^5$ (in SI units)
questions.explanation:
$\begin{aligned} & \ell=2 \mathrm{~m} ; \mathrm{Y}=2 \times 10^{11} \frac{\mathrm{~N}}{\mathrm{~m}^2} \\ & \begin{aligned} \mu=-\frac{\left(\frac{\Delta \mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{r}}\right)}{\left(\frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}\right)} \Rightarrow \frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell} & =\frac{1}{\mu} \times\left(\frac{\Delta \mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{r}}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{0.2} \times\left(10^{-3}\right)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}=5 \times 10^{-3} \\ & \begin{aligned} \mathrm{u}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{y} \varepsilon_{\ell}^2 & =\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10^{11} \times\left[5 \times 10^{-3}\right]^2 \\ & =25\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$$

questions.question: A cylindrical rod of length 1 m and radius 4 cm is mounted vertically. It is subjected to a shear force of $10^5 \mathrm{~N}$ at the top. Considering infinitesimally small displacement in the upper edge, the angular displacement $\theta$ of the rod axis from its original position would be : (shear moduli, $\left.\mathrm{G}=10^{10} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2\right)$
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \text { Shear moduli }=\frac{\sigma_{\text {shear }}}{\theta} \\ & 10^{10}=\frac{10^5}{\pi \times 16 \times 10^{-4}} \times \frac{1}{\theta} \\ & \theta=\frac{1}{160 \pi} \text { Radian }\end{aligned}$

questions.question: A square aluminium (shear modulus is $25 \times {10}^{9}{\mathrm{Nm}}^{ - 2}$) slab of side $60\mathrm{cm}$ and thickness $15\mathrm{cm}$ is subjected to a shearing force (on its narrow face) of $18.0 \times {10}^{4}N$. The lower edge is riveted to the floor. The displacement of the upper edge is _____ $\mu m$.
questions.explanation:
Shearing stress is given by $\frac{F}{A} = \eta \frac{x}{l}$

Thus, displacement is $x = \frac{Fl}{A\eta } \implies x = \frac{18 \times {10}^{4} \times 60 \times {10}^{ - 2}}{60 \times {10}^{ - 2} \times 15 \times {10}^{ - 2} \times 25 \times {10}^{9}} = 48 \times {10}^{ - 6}m = 48\mu m$

questions.question: Two slabs with square cross section of different materials $(1,2)$ with equal sides $(l)$ and thickness $\mathrm{d}_1$ and $\mathrm{d}_2$ such that $\mathrm{d}_2=2 \mathrm{~d}_1$ and $l \gt \mathrm{d}_2$. Considering lower edges of these slabs are fixed to the floor, we apply equal shearing force on the narrow faces. The angle of deformation is $\theta_2=2 \theta_1$. If the shear moduli of material 1 is $4 \times 10^9 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$, then shear moduli of material 2 is $\mathrm{x} \times 10^9 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$, where value of $x$ is ________.
questions.explanation: Deformation angle $\begin{aligned} & 2 $\$theta_1 =$\$theta_2 \\ & $\Rightarrow$ 2 $\frac{\$sigma_1$}{\$eta_1$} = \frac{\$sigma_2$}{\$eta_2$}$ \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2\left(\frac{\mathrm{~F}}{\ell \mathrm{~d}_1 \eta_1}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\ell \mathrm{d}_2 \eta_2} \\ & \Rightarrow \eta_2=\frac{\eta_1}{4}=1 \times 10^9 \Rightarrow x=1\end{aligned}$
